subfield: Condensed matter and materials physics / photovoltaics
motivation: Miyasaka first used organometal halide perovskites as light absorbers in photovoltaic cells (2009). Park demonstrated the first stable solid-state perovskite cell with about 9% efficiency (2012). Snaith showed that perovskites act as ambipolar semiconductors with long carrier diffusion lengths and work in simple planar heterojunctions (2012–2013), removing the need for a mesoporous scaffold. These results opened a new class of solution-processable semiconductors with sharp absorption edges, tunable bandgaps, defect tolerance and unusual carrier physics. Single-junction cell efficiencies rose from 3.8% to over 26% in about fifteen years, faster than any other photovoltaic material, and perovskite–silicon tandems now exceed 34%. In-situ synchrotron and neutron studies of their structural dynamics and ion migration have helped make this a fruitful field for basic condensed-matter physics. Commercial tandem modules are now being made, a direct contribution to the energy transition.
